name: The Rieseneiche of the Sauerbusch

location.address: Sauerbusch, Dresdner Heide (forest district Hofewiese), near Langebruck

access: Free. Public forest (Sachsenforst, Dresdner Heide); a signposted educational trail 'Rieseneichen' (run by the Heimatverein Weixdorf) leads to it. Forest paths, no ticket.
transport: Not verified. Remote forest stand in the far north-east of the Heide near Langebruck, well over 30 minutes from the centre; reached on foot or by bike from Langebruck or Weixdorf. Check current timetables before quoting a stop.
verify_notes: Register-only (city Naturdenkmal ND 72; de.wikipedia plus Wikidata coordinate). Tree-level Wikidata coordinate; Commons has CC0 photos of the trunk base and hole taken 2021-05-31 by Pedalito (CC0), so a photo exists; lifecheck RECENT 2025-06-12 near the pin. Conflict on height: de.wikipedia article says about 22 m, the ND list says 14 m; main stem broke off at about 15 m, the crown is single limbs. Girth about 6.60 m at 1.30 m (measured 2016, cited to monumentaltrees on the list page; cross-checked on article). Age 'up to 700 years' is an estimate in the article, not a measured date; keep vague. History: 1679 forest protocol lists two oaks in the Sauerbusch as boundary markers, likely mast trees; both protected 1938 (other sources say 1958); the second oak fell in a fire started by children in 1993. The forest district describes the tree as 'in its last stage of life' although vital; stem has heavy overgrowth, one side nearly debarked, parts stabilised with concrete. Alive as of 2021 photos; recheck. Twin folded: none (the second oak is gone). Lead: a 'Dresdner Heide' walk with the Rotbuche dre_007 (about 5.5 km apart, separate stops).
story:
In 1679 a forest protocol listed two oaks in the Sauerbusch as boundary markers. One of them is still alive. Its main stem broke off at about fifteen metres long ago, so what stands now is a trunk about 6.60 metres round carrying a crown made of single limbs. The local account puts it at up to 700 years, which is an estimate rather than a count; somewhere between four and seven centuries is the honest reading.

The two oaks were probably mast trees, kept for their acorns, and both were placed under protection in 1938, although some sources give 1958. In 1993 a fire started by children killed the second one. This one carried on.

It has not carried on easily. The forest district describes it as being in the last stage of its life, although it is still vital. Heavy growth covers the stem, one side is almost stripped of bark, and parts of it are held together with concrete. Even its height is disputed: the Wikipedia article says about 22 metres, the city's natural monument list says 14.

A signposted trail, the Rieseneichen path kept by the heritage society in Weixdorf, leads through the far north-east of the Dresdner Heide to the trunk. It is a forest walk from Langebruck or Weixdorf rather than a city stroll, and this oak is the reason to make it.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the snapped-off main stem on a trunk about 6.60 metres round, one side almost bare of bark and patched with concrete. It stands on the signposted Rieseneichen trail in the Sauerbusch.

name: The Rotbuche of the Dresdner Heide

location.address: Dresdner Heide, forest section 109 (Revier Langebruck), about 150 m north-west of the crossing of Radeberger Strasse and Schneise 8

access: Free. Stands in the public forest of the Dresdner Heide (Sachsenforst), a short way off the Schneise 8 forest ride; no entry charge.
transport: Not verified. Inside the Heide, over 30 minutes from the centre; reached on foot from the Radeberger Strasse side. Check timetables before quoting a stop.
verify_notes: Register only (city Naturdenkmal ND 108, designated Dec 2000). Wikidata coordinate 51.09819,13.849767 agrees with the de.wikipedia description (150 m NW of the Radeberger Strasse / Schneise 8 crossing) only in prose, which I did not measure, so precision is stated approximate. Photos on Commons: CC BY-SA 3.0 by Dr. Bernd Gross (2015-05-26, 22 files) and CC BY-SA 4.0 Staubi59 (2017). lifecheck on the pin returned NONE. Measurements at designation in 2000: height about 35 m, girth 5.70 m, crown diameter about 28 m. After an unseen fork defect plus a hurricane in October 2002 more than a third of the crown broke off, so today's tree is lower and lopsided; the 35 m figure is the pre-2002 height. The photos show the tree after the damage, which a writer should check. Age 250 years was an estimate in 2000. At designation only the beech behind the Weisses Schloss in Cossebaude (ND 66) was a bigger beech in Dresden. Protected zone 18 m around the trunk.
story:
In October 2002 a hurricane found a fork in this beech that nobody knew was failing, and more than a third of the crown came down. Two years earlier Dresden had made it a natural monument, measured at about 35 metres tall, 5.70 metres round and with a crown some 28 metres across. At that point only one beech in the city was bigger, the one behind the Weisses Schloss in Cossebaude.

What stands in forest section 109 of the Dresdner Heide today is the tree that came out of that storm: lower than the 35 metres in the record and lopsided where the crown went. Every photograph on file was taken after the damage, so they show the beech as a visitor will meet it rather than as it looked on the day it was designated.

The age given in 2000 was about 250 years, and that was an estimate then. Add the years since and it lands somewhere around 275, give or take a few decades. The ordinance protects a ring of 18 metres around the trunk along with the tree itself.

It stands a short way into the forest, about 150 metres north-west of the point where Radeberger Strasse crosses the forest ride called Schneise 8. Our pin is approximate, so expect to look around for the broken crown once you reach the crossing.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the lopsided crown, more than a third of it lost to a storm in 2002, above a trunk about 5.70 metres round. It stands about 150 metres north-west of where Radeberger Strasse crosses Schneise 8.

name: The Oak of Barnsdorfer Strasse

location.address: Junction of Weinbohlaer Strasse and Barnsdorfer Strasse, Leipziger Vorstadt

access: Free. A freestanding tree at a street junction on public ground.
transport: Not verified in detail; inner-city district north-west of the Neustadt, on the B170 side near Hansastrasse. Check the nearest tram stop before quoting.
verify_notes: Register only (city Naturdenkmal ND 29, protected 3 Jan 1985, resolution 266/85). Tree-level Wikidata coordinate; de.wikipedia places it at the southern fork of Weinbohlaer and Barnsdorfer Strasse, about 100 m south-east of the Hechtstrasse turn-off from Hansastrasse, which fits the pin. Photos: 8 files CC BY-SA 3.0 Dr. Bernd Gross, 2015-05-20. lifecheck on the pin returned NONE and the newest photo is 2015, so alive confirmation is thin: flagged. Height about 25 m, crown about 30 m, girth 4.45 m (register). Planted about 1880, probably in the beer garden of the pub 'Zur Gruenen Aue' on the road tip, which stood until 1960 (article says 'vermutlich', so keep hedged; do not bridge it into fact). About 150 m north-east, in the St.-Pauli-Friedhof, stand the Marschall oak and Meschwitz oak, planted c.1870/80 and treated as Dresden memorial trees (Wikidata Q109422836, Q124842660): possible cluster, not verified as accessible here. Protected the same day as the Doebelner Strasse oak, the Kaditzer Linde (dre_005) and the Heide pine.
story:
This oak probably started out in a beer garden. It was planted around 1880 on the tip of land where Weinbohlaer Strasse and Barnsdorfer Strasse fork, and the pub on that tip, Zur Gruenen Aue, stood until 1960. The written record says the tree was probably part of the pub's garden, and nobody has managed to get further than probably. The pub is gone. The oak, about 140 years old, has outlasted it by more than sixty years.

It has grown to about 25 metres with a crown some 30 metres wide, and its trunk measures 4.45 metres round. Dresden made it a natural monument on 3 January 1985, the same day the city protected the Kaditzer Linde, an oak on Doebelner Strasse and a pine in the Heide.

About 150 metres to the north-east, in the St.-Pauli-Friedhof, stand two more oaks of the same generation, the Marschall oak and the Meschwitz oak, planted around 1870 or 1880 and treated by the city as memorial trees. We have not checked how freely the cemetery can be walked, so this page sends you only to the junction.

The newest photographs of this oak date from 2015, and we have no recent confirmation that it is still in good health. If you pass the fork and it is standing, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the freestanding oak, 4.45 metres round, on the tip of land where Weinbohlaer Strasse and Barnsdorfer Strasse fork. It stands about 100 metres south-east of where Hechtstrasse leaves Hansastrasse.

name: The Linden on the Laubegast Riverbank

location.address: Laubegaster Ufer, by house no. 17, Altlaubegast

access: Free. Stands on the outside of the ice-protection wall of Laubegaster Ufer 17, beside the road; just north of the driveway the road is closed to cars and is a foot and cycle path forming part of the left-bank Elbe cycle route.
transport: Not verified; Laubegast is an eastern Elbe-bank district. Check the nearest tram stop and walking time before quoting.
verify_notes: Register (city Naturdenkmal ND 89, protected 10 June 1999) plus the owner's 1997 letter quoted on de.wikipedia. Coordinates: de.wikipedia list 51/1/30.95N 13/50/23.9E (=51.02582, 13.83997), Wikidata Q124719169 51.0253,13.839993; they agree within about 70 m, so I used the list value which is described as 'by Nr. 17'; stated confirmed because the tree is on the Elbe path next to a named house, but a writer could re-read the Wikidata offset. Alive: Commons photo 2025-12-27 by Z thomas (CC BY 4.0) and 2024-05-09 lifecheck RECENT. Girth 3.90 m, height about 20 m, crown about 16 m. Age: article says planted or sown in the second half of the 17th century, narrowing to the 1670s or 1680, and the owner wrote of a '320 year old' linden in 1997. The owner built a protective masonry surround in 1913. In March 1940 the largest Elbe flood of the 20th century drove 40 cm ice floes against the wall and tree for 10 to 15 hours, leaving a wound about 50 cm tall around half the trunk; a ridge at roughly 1.5 m height still shows it. Pavement around the roots was replaced with cobbles to protect it. The house behind was built 1879 for a Saxon court marshal (protected Kulturdenkmal). Two other Laubegast ND trees stand about 500 m each way (black poplars at no. 1, black pine at no. 39), same cycle path. Photos CC BY-SA 3.0 Dr. Bernd Gross 2014/2015.
story:
In March 1940 the biggest Elbe flood of the twentieth century drove ice floes 40 centimetres thick against this lime for ten to fifteen hours. The floes hit both the tree and the masonry surround its owner had built in 1913. The ice tore a wound about half a metre tall around half the trunk, and the ridge it left still shows at roughly 1.5 metres up.

The lime was already old by then. The local account has it planted or sown in the second half of the seventeenth century, most likely in the 1670s or around 1680, and in 1997 the owner wrote of a 320-year-old linden. That puts it somewhere near 340 today. The house behind it at number 17 is a youngster by comparison, built in 1879 for a Saxon court marshal and now a listed monument in its own right.

It is a small-leaved lime, about 20 metres tall with a trunk 3.90 metres round, standing outside the ice-protection wall beside the road. The paving over its roots was replaced with cobbles to protect them, and the city made it a natural monument in June 1999.

Just north of the driveway the road closes to cars and becomes part of the Elbe cycle route, and two more protected trees stand about 500 metres away in each direction along it: black poplars at number 1 and a black pine at number 39.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the old ice wound, a ridge at about 1.5 metres on a trunk 3.90 metres round. It stands by the road outside the wall of Laubegaster Ufer 17.

best_time.label: July, when it flowers and the riverbank smells of lime blossom

name: The Fluttering Elm of Konigsbrucker Strasse

location.address: Konigsbrucker Strasse 49, on the pavement side between houses 49 and 51, Aussere Neustadt

access: Free. The elm stands on the pavement side of the property in front of the houses at Konigsbrucker Strasse 49 to 51 and is visible and reachable from the public pavement on a main street; the pin marks the tree on the street frontage.
transport: Not verified in detail; Aussere Neustadt on the Konigsbrucker Strasse tram corridor, close to the centre. Check the nearest stop before quoting.
verify_notes: Register (city Naturdenkmal ND 131, ordinance January 2015). Wikidata coordinate 51.07062119,13.74958807 matches the ND list value 51/4/14.05N 13/44/59.05E (=51.07057, 13.74974), two independent entries within about 15 m. Photos: 5 files CC BY-SA 3.0 Z thomas 2018-05-28 and 7 files 2019-05-06/07, plus Dr. Bernd Gross 2015. lifecheck says OLD (2011 file) but the Commons upload dates show 2018/2019; newest photo 2019, so alive-now is thin: flagged. Measurements per de.wikipedia: height about 30 m, crown about 20 m, girth 3.57 m. Why it was chosen: in the early 2010s the city put forward 39 especially valuable trees at 29 sites for protection; this elm was picked because European elm species are threatened by Dutch elm disease from Asian fungi and this exceptional specimen is healthy and defines the streetscape. Flatter-Ulme Altubigau and the Sachsenplatz elms had been protected since 1999. No age is documented; leave empty and let the page ask. Possible access caveat: the tree is on the property frontage 'gehwegseitig vorgelagert' (pavement-side), which I read as public pavement; I could not check the plot boundary on the ground.
story:
Dresden protected this elm in 2015 for surviving something most of its kind have not. Dutch elm disease, spread by fungi that arrived from Asia, has killed elms across Europe, and when the city went looking in the early 2010s for its most valuable trees, 39 of them at 29 sites, it picked this European white elm as an exceptional specimen that was still healthy.

It is not a park tree. It stands on Konigsbrucker Strasse in the Aussere Neustadt, on the pavement side in front of numbers 49 and 51, and it sets the look of the street: about 30 metres tall, with a crown some 20 metres across and a trunk 3.57 metres round. Trams run past it along the Konigsbrucker Strasse corridor.

It was not the city's first protected elm. A white elm in Altubigau and the elms on Sachsenplatz had been natural monuments since 1999, so this one joined a short list rather than starting it.

Two things we do not know. Nobody has documented when it was planted, so this page gives no age; if you know, tell us. And the newest photographs on record are from 2019, so if you walk past and it is still standing over the pavement, that is worth a message too.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the tall elm, about 30 metres, on the pavement side of Konigsbrucker Strasse in front of numbers 49 and 51. Its trunk measures 3.57 metres round.
